newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone's neighbours back dialogue, sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone's neighbours back dialogue, sanctions.

text.p: Sierra Leone's neighbours opted on Friday for dialogue and economic sanctions to persuade its military rulers to reinstate ousted civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah but retained the option of military force.
But West African foreign ministers, meeting in Guinea's capital Conakry, recommended such measures be subject to prior consultations "at the highest level".
In Freetown, a spokesman for the ruling military junta said it was open to negotiations about the return of Kabbah as president to the former British colony.

The strategy to restore Kabbah, thrashed out by foreign ministers of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) at a meeting that ran into the early hours of Friday, was outlined in a 16-point communique.
The ministers stressed that no country should recognise the regime that emerged from the May 25 coup.
They recommended working "to restore legitimate government through a combination of three measures -- dialogue, sanctions and an embargo as well as recourse to force."
But they added: "In order to increase the effectiveness of the above measures, the ministers... recommended prior consultations among member states at the highest level."

In Freetown, Armed Forces Revolutionary Council spokesman Colonel Abdul Sesay said it welcomed dialogue. "Who drove Tejan Kabbah away? We did not drive Kabbah away. The AFRC is open to negotiations about his return as president to Sierra Leone."

A committee of Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea and Ivory Coast plus ECOWAS and the Organisation of African Unity has been set up to implement the decisions. One diplomatic source said it would begin the dialogue and report back to the ECOWAS chairman, Nigeria's military ruler Sani Abacha, within two weeks.

Junior military officers toppled Kabbah on May 25 accusing him of stalling on peace with rebels, who took up arms in 1991, and of promoting ethnic hatred and humilitating the army by arming Kamajor traditional hunters to act as a civil militia.

Nigeria had troops in Sierra Leone under a defence pact before the coup and on June 2 its gunboats shelled the capital Freetown in a show of force, triggering clashes with Sierra Leone soldiers and rebels. It has reinforced its troops there.
Diplomats said it held out for keeping the military option.
Kabbah took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule. They took place despite civil war and without cooperation of the rebels.
The Revolutionary United Front rebels rallied to the coup, the third in five years. Kamajor leaders have so far rejected offers of a place in a government of national unity.
The OAU annual summit in Zimbabwe in early June denounced the coup and called for the restoration of Kabbah.
Military ruler Major Johnny Paul Koroma said on Wednesday Kabbah could return but spoke of organising fresh elections.
Officials of the ruling military junta earlier called for an all-party national conference, with Kabbah taking part, to discuss the future of the country and organisation of elections.

Witnesses and officials say Nigerian gunboats have begun a sea blockade of Sierra Leone by turning away ships. Oil industry sources said on Tuesday there was two-weeks' supply left to keep Sierra Leone's power station running.
Ivory Coast sponsored the peace deal with the rebels which Kabbah and rebel leader Foday Sankoh signed in its commercial capital Abidjan in November.

The U.N. World Food Programme said in Conakry on Thursday a humanitarian crisis was brewing in Sierra Leone. "We need to be able to move relief food without interference from armed elements," spokesman Mohamed Diab said.
